name: Leuprolide
summary: A prescription hormone-blocking injection that switches off the body's sex-hormone production, used for prostate cancer, endometriosis, fibroids and early puberty in children.
what_it_is: Leuprolide is a lab-made drug that acts like gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), the signal that drives the pituitary gland's control of the testes and ovaries. Given continuously as a long-acting injection, it first causes a short rise in testosterone or estrogen, which can briefly worsen symptoms, and then shuts their production down to very low levels. The effect is meant to reverse after stopping; the label says normal function usually returns within three months.

evidence.why: It is FDA-approved for advanced prostate cancer, endometriosis, fibroid-related anemia before surgery and central precocious puberty, based on the clinical trials reviewed for its labels.

status_us.label: FDA-approved prescription drug
status_us.note: Approved as Lupron Depot and Eligard for advanced prostate cancer, as a separate Lupron Depot product for endometriosis and for fibroid-related anemia before surgery, and as Lupron Depot-PED and Fensolvi for central precocious puberty in children.

benefits.claim: Lowers testosterone to castration levels, usually within four weeks, in men with advanced prostate cancer
Hormone-lowering therapy for prostate cancer (not leuprolide alone) cut prostate-cancer deaths and deaths from any cause in a pooled analysis of 11 randomized trials
Relieves pain and shrinks lesions in women with endometriosis
Improves anemia before surgery in women with fibroids, used together with iron
Pauses early puberty in children aged 2 and older with central precocious puberty

risks.risk: Hot flashes and sweats, in about half or more of users in trials

Tumor flare in men with prostate cancer: testosterone first rises about 50% in the first weeks, which can worsen bone pain, nerve symptoms, blood in the urine or bladder blockage; spinal cord compression with paralysis can occur
Lower sex drive, erection problems and testicular shrinkage, expected while testosterone is suppressed (testicular shrinkage in about 20% at one strength in trials)
Bone loss: in women, spine bone density fell an average of about 6% after a year without add-back hormone, and some loss may not recover; bone loss is also reported in men
Depression or mood swings (about 1 in 5 women in endometriosis trials); crying, irritability and aggression are reported in children
Higher blood sugar, new or worse diabetes, and higher blood fats

Heart attack, sudden cardiac death, stroke and a longer QT interval (a heart-rhythm measure) have been linked to it in men; the label calls the risk low, and a pooled analysis of trials found no rise in heart deaths
Rare serious reports: seizures, pituitary apoplexy (sudden headache, vomiting, vision changes), severe skin reactions, and in children pseudotumor cerebri (raised pressure inside the skull)

avoid_if: Pregnancy: it can harm a developing baby
Known allergy to leuprolide or other GnRH drugs
Osteoporosis or strong risk factors for bone loss (needs a clinician's review first)
Heart disease, long QT syndrome, diabetes or a seizure history (needs a clinician's review first)
interactions: Other drugs that prolong the QT interval: the label advises weighing the risks first
Bupropion and SSRI antidepressants: seizures have been reported with combined use
Lab tests of pituitary and sex-hormone function can be thrown off during use and for up to three months after

before: Blood glucose or HbA1c and a lipid panel
Bone density before any repeat course in women
ECG and electrolytes if heart risk factors are present
during: Blood glucose or HbA1c and lipids
ECG and electrolytes periodically in people at risk
In children: LH or sex-hormone levels, height growth and bone age
labs.why: The labels use these to confirm hormones are suppressed and to catch effects on blood sugar, blood fats, heart rhythm, bone and growth.

studies.title: Association of androgen deprivation therapy with cardiovascular death in patients with prostate cancer: a meta-analysis of randomized trials
studies.people: 4,805 men with prostate cancer in 11 randomized trials
studies.finding: Hormone-lowering therapy did not raise cardiovascular deaths (11.0% vs 11.2%) and was linked to fewer prostate-cancer deaths and fewer deaths overall.

studies.title: Diabetes and cardiovascular disease during androgen deprivation therapy: observational study of veterans with prostate cancer
studies.finding: Men treated with GnRH agonists had higher rates of diabetes (about 28% higher), coronary heart disease, heart attack, sudden cardiac death and stroke than men not on hormone therapy.

studies.title: LUPRON DEPOT (leuprolide acetate for depot suspension) prescribing information, endometriosis and fibroids
studies.people: Women with endometriosis or fibroids in clinical trials
studies.finding: Hot flashes affected 73 to 84% of women; spine bone density fell an average of 6.3% after 52 weeks without add-back therapy, and some loss persisted after treatment ended.

ask_your_clinician: What will we do to protect my bones, and do I need a bone density scan or add-back hormone?
How will we check my blood sugar, cholesterol and heart rhythm while I'm on it?
Which symptoms should make me call you right away?

notes_for_editor: All main uses are approved indications; using leuprolide for general 'hormone balance' is not an approved use and no evidence for it was found. Off-label uses (for example in fertility treatment) were not sourced because NCBI Bookshelf and PubMed pages blocked automated fetching, so they are left out. Heart-risk evidence is mixed: a large observational cohort found more heart disease and diabetes, while a meta-analysis of randomized trials found no rise in cardiovascular deaths. Label risk frequencies for diabetes and heart events are not given, so how_common is 'unknown'.
